subject: Anthropology
title: Reciprocity
description: A short lesson to help you apply Reciprocity.

hook.text: You give a gift. Your friend gives one back. But this isn't just niceness — it's one of humanity's oldest economies.

buildup.text: Reciprocity is the exchange of goods and services between people based on social obligation, not market pricing.

discovery.text: Sahlins identified three types: generalized (free giving), balanced (equal return), and negative (seeking advantage).

twist.text: A gift creates a debt. Reciprocity isn't free — it builds alliances, creates obligations, and sustains social bonds.

climax.text: Reciprocity shows that exchange existed long before markets. Humans traded favors before they ever traded goods.

punchline.text: Every gift is also a social contract.

quiz.question: What is generalized reciprocity?
options: Free giving without expecting immediate return

details.summary: Reciprocity is exchange between individuals or groups governed by social obligation rather than market price. Marshall Sahlins distinguished generalized (free giving), balanced (expected equal return), and negative (attempting unequal advantage) reciprocity based on social distance.
details.whyItMatters: Reciprocity shows that exchange is fundamentally social, not just economic. Understanding how social distance determines exchange behavior reveals the moral foundations underlying all economies, including modern market systems.
takeaways: Reciprocity is exchange governed by social obligation, not price
Sahlins identified generalized, balanced, and negative types
Social distance determines which type of reciprocity applies

faq.question: How does social distance affect reciprocity?
faq.answer: Close kin receive generalized reciprocity — sharing without expectation of return. More distant relations involve balanced reciprocity — exchange of equivalent value. Strangers and enemies get negative reciprocity — attempts to maximize personal advantage through bargaining or deception.

faq.question: Is reciprocity still relevant in market economies?
faq.answer: Absolutely. Gift-giving, favors at work, neighborly help, and informal exchanges follow reciprocity logic. Even in market societies, most daily interactions involve social reciprocity rather than market transactions. People keep mental accounts of social debts.
